notes.meaning: Elijah suddenly appears before King Ahab and announces that there will be no dew or rain for years except at his word. Ahab had led the nation into worshiping Baal, a false storm god whom the people believed controlled the weather. By shutting off the rain, the true God showed that He alone controls nature and rules over all kings.

God gives Elijah a direct message telling him to leave immediately and hide by the Brook of Cherith, east of the Jordan River. Ahab would soon search everywhere to arrest the prophet or force him to end the drought. God led Elijah away to keep him safe and to teach him quiet dependence on the Lord.

God promises that Elijah will have fresh water to drink from the stream and commands ravens to bring him food. Ravens are wild birds that do not even share food with their own young, yet God commanded them to care for His prophet. This showed Elijah that the Lord can use any part of creation to supply our needs.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars propose that the Hebrew word translated as ravens might instead refer to Arab nomads, traveling merchants, or people from a nearby town called Oreb.

notes.meaning: Elijah immediately obeys God and goes to live in isolation by the Brook of Cherith. He does not question the unusual instructions or delay his journey. True faith is shown when we promptly follow God's direction even when the road ahead seems uncertain.

The ravens bring Elijah bread and meat every morning and evening, while the brook gives him clean water. God gave him daily meals just like He once provided manna in the desert for the Israelites. Elijah learned to trust the Lord for each day's food rather than relying on stored-up supplies.

After some time, the brook dries up completely because there has been no rain anywhere in the land. The drought Elijah announced affected his own water supply just like everyone else's. God allowed the stream to dry up so Elijah would know it was time to move on to the next chapter of God's plan.

The Lord tells Elijah to pack up and travel to Zarephath in Sidon, where God has commanded a widow to provide for him. Zarephath was in foreign Phoenician territory, the very home region of wicked Queen Jezebel and the center of Baal worship. God proved His supreme authority by sheltering His prophet right in enemy territory through a poor, helpless widow.

Elijah walks to Zarephath and meets a widow gathering sticks outside the city gate, asking her for a drink of water in a cup. The fact that she was picking up a few stray sticks showed she was deeply impoverished and had no servants. Her willingness to share water during a severe drought showed a kind and generous heart.

As the woman walks off to get the water, Elijah calls out and asks her to bring him a piece of bread as well. Both food and water were very scarce because the drought had spread across Phoenicia too. Elijah asked for bread to test her willingness and to confirm that she was the woman God chose to support him.

The widow explains that she has no baked bread at all, only a single handful of flour in an earthen jar and a drop of oil in a jug. She was gathering sticks to cook one last bite for herself and her son before they starved to death. By swearing by the living Lord, she showed respect for Elijah's God while laying bare her complete desperation.

Elijah tells the woman not to fear, but asks her to bake a small loaf for him first before making food for herself and her child. This sounded like an unreasonable request to make of a starving mother. It was a major test of faith, inviting her to trust God's promise by putting the Lord's messenger first.

Elijah announces God's promise that her jar of flour will not run out and her jug of oil will not dry up until rain returns. The Lord promised to provide a constant supply of daily bread all through the famine. God honors those who step out in faith and trust His word in hard times.

The widow trusts Elijah's words, bakes the bread for him first, and her entire household has food to eat day after day. She chose to give away her very last meal on the strength of God's promise. Because of her remarkable faith, God supplied all their needs for months to come.

The flour jar never empties and the oil jug never runs dry, fulfilling every word the Lord spoke through Elijah. God did not fill a giant storehouse all at once, but gave fresh supplies each day as they used them. This ongoing miracle proved that the God of Israel has total power over life and food even in a land devoted to idols.

Some time later, the widow's son falls very sick, grows weaker, and finally stops breathing. Even though this family had seen God supply daily food, they were not spared from painful sickness and grief. The boy's death was a crushing loss that tested the faith of both the widow and the prophet.

In deep anguish, the mother asks Elijah if he came to bring attention to her past sins and cause her child to die. People in the ancient world commonly assumed that personal tragedies were direct punishments from God for specific sins. Having a holy prophet in her home made her painfully aware of her own shortcomings, and she thought God was punishing her.

Elijah gently tells the mother to give him her son, takes the dead boy from her arms, and carries him up to his own bed. He did not scold her for her bitter words, but acted with tender care. Elijah brought the boy to his private upper room so he could pray to God without interruption.

Elijah cries out in earnest prayer, asking the Lord why He allowed such tragedy to fall on the widow who had kindly opened her home to him. The prophet poured out his honest grief and confusion before God. He pleaded for mercy by reminding the Lord of the widow's generous care and deep suffering.

Elijah stretches himself over the boy's body three times and begs God to let the child's life return to him. This intense action showed Elijah's deep compassion and his desperate longing for God's life-giving power to touch the dead boy. Elijah had no Bible story of someone being raised from the dead to look back on, yet he prayed with bold faith.

The Lord answers Elijah's cry, the breath of life returns into the child, and he revives. This is the very first resurrection recorded in the Bible. God showed that His power reaches even beyond the grave, proving that the Lord alone holds authority over life and death.

Elijah carries the living child down from the upper room and gives him back to his mother, joyfully announcing that her son is alive. This wonderful reunion turned her crushing grief into pure joy. God rewarded the widow's hospitality and publicly confirmed Elijah as His chosen messenger.

The woman confesses that she now knows for sure that Elijah is a man of God and that the Lord's word from his mouth is the truth. Her earlier doubts disappeared in the light of her son's resurrection. Even though she grew up among idol worshipers, this miracle led her to place her full trust in the living God of Israel.
